title: Springs, Seals & Keys
summary: Helical spring rate and Wahl stress factor, O-ring gland design, and key joint shear/crushing checks for shafts.

sections.heading: Small Elements, Big Responsibilities
sections.content: Springs, seals, and keys are the "small parts" that decide whether a machine **returns** to its position, **keeps its fluid**, and **transmits its torque**. They are cheap, ubiquitous, and — precisely because they are treated as trivial — a common source of field failures: a spring that sags, an O-ring that extrudes, a key that shears. Each is a designed element with real formulas behind it.

sections.heading: Helical Compression Spring Rate
sections.content:
A helical spring's **rate** (force per unit deflection) for round wire is:

$$k = \frac{G d^4}{8 D^3 N_a}$$

with $G$ the shear modulus (79.3 GPa for steel), $d$ wire diameter, $D$ mean coil diameter, $N_a$ active coils.

Example — $G = 79.3$ GPa, $d = 3$ mm, $D = 20$ mm, $N_a = 8$:

$$k = \frac{79\,300 \times 3^4}{8 \times 20^3 \times 8} = \frac{6.42 \times 10^6}{512\,000} = 12.5 \text{ N/mm}$$

Note the sensitivity: rate scales with $d^4$ and $1/D^3$ — a 10% wire-diameter change alters the rate by ~46%. Never order "springs like that one" without the wire size on the drawing. Design limits: the spring must not exceed its **solid length** (all coils touching) at maximum deflection, and buckling must be checked when free length / mean diameter exceeds ~4.

sections.heading: Stress & the Wahl Factor
sections.content:
Direct shear plus the **curvature effect** on the inside of the coil raise the maximum shear stress. The correction is the **Wahl factor**:

$$K_w = \frac{4C-1}{4C-4} + \frac{0.615}{C}$$

where the spring index $C = D/d$ (typical 4–12; below ~4 the spring is hard to wind, above ~12 it is unstable). The corrected stress:

$$\tau = K_w \, \frac{8 F D}{\pi d^3} \, \leq \, \tau_{allow}$$

Check **fatigue** with $\tau_{min} \to \tau_{max}$ cycling (springs cycle in service far more than they are statically loaded — see [[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|fatigue]]), and for compression springs verify bucking stability and set (permanent set removal) by **scragging** — pre-compressing to solid to stabilize the free length.

sections.heading: O-Rings & Seal Design
sections.content:
An O-ring seals by **radial squeeze**: installed, it deforms a controlled amount and the fluid pressure pushes it against the groove wall. Gland design rules:

- **Squeeze 15–25%** of the cross-section for static seals; less (~10%) for dynamic (low friction), more with low-temperature or vacuum service.
- **Gland fill** — the groove volume must exceed the O-ring volume (typically 75–90% fill) so pressure does not hydraulically burst the ring.
- **Extrusion gap** — keep the radial clearance ≤ 0.1 mm at max pressure, or add **backup rings**; hot, high-pressure fluid extrudes unsupported O-rings through the gap.
- Diameter stretch 2–5% (never more than 5% for NBR/FKM; silicone tolerates more), and cut the groove for a **hard**, fine-finished seat (Ra ≤ 0.8 µm, no spiral machining marks) so the seal does not leak along its own groove.

Material: NBR (nitrile) for oils/water, FKM (Viton) for temperature and chemicals, EPDM for water/brake fluid but never oil. Dynamic rod seals (hydraulics) are covered by the same squeeze logic plus a wiper/scraper in front.

sections.heading: Keys: Shear & Crushing
sections.content:
A **parallel key** transmits torque from shaft to hub through shear on the key cross-section and crushing on the flank:

$$\tau = \frac{2T}{d \, b \, l} \, \leq \, \tau_{allow}, \qquad \sigma_c = \frac{4T}{d \, h \, l} \, \leq \, \sigma_{c,allow}$$

with $d$ shaft diameter, $b$ key width, $h$ key height, $l$ key length.

Example — $T = 200$ N·m, $d = 30$ mm, key 8×7, length 40 mm:

$$\tau = \frac{2 \times 200\,000}{30 \times 8 \times 40} = 41.7 \text{ MPa}, \qquad \sigma_c = \frac{4 \times 200\,000}{30 \times 7 \times 40} = 95.2 \text{ MPa}$$

Design guidance: shear usually governs for **soft** keys, crush for hardened hubs; standard key sizes follow shaft diameter ($b \approx d/4$); keyway **stress concentration** at the shaft corner is typically the real limiter on fatigue-loaded shafts — prefer involute splines or press fits (see [[bearings-and-shafts|bearings & shafts]]) when torque is high and cyclic. Multiple keys do NOT multiply capacity linearly — the first key carries the majority; use one properly sized key instead.

keyTakeaways: Spring rate k = G·d⁴/(8D³·N_a): d⁴ and 1/D³ sensitivity means wire size must be on the drawing.
Apply the Wahl factor for curved-wire stress; check solid length, buckling, and fatigue cycling.
O-rings need 15–25% squeeze, ≤90% gland fill, extrusion-gap control, and smooth (Ra ≤ 0.8 µm) groove seats.
Keys are sized by shear and crushing checks; the keyway stress concentration usually governs fatigue shafts.
